blocks.content: Deadlock is one of the most important failure modes in concurrent systems. This chapter introduces the idea at a basic level, as a seed within Synchronization and Concurrency, so you can recognize the pattern the moment you see it.

A dedicated Deadlocks module elsewhere in this course covers prevention, avoidance, the Bankers Algorithm, and detection and recovery in full depth. Here the goal is simpler: understand precisely what a deadlock is, see the classic two thread example, and know how it differs from a process that is merely slow.
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785408559202-347506379.png
1. What Is a Deadlock

A set of two or more processes is deadlocked when each process in the set is waiting for a resource that is held by another process in the same set. Because every process is waiting on another, none of them can ever make progress. Without help from outside the set, such as an operating system or a database killing one of the processes, this standstill lasts forever.

blocks.title: In one sentence
blocks.content: A deadlock is a permanent, unrecoverable standstill in which every process in a set is waiting for a resource held by another process in that same set.
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785408559203-691860201.png
2. A Simple Concrete Example: Two Threads, Two Locks
blocks.text: 2. A Simple Concrete Example: Two Threads, Two Locks

blocks.content: The smallest and most common deadlock involves just two threads and two locks. Thread A acquires Lock 1 and then tries to acquire Lock 2. Thread B acquires Lock 2 and then tries to acquire Lock 1. If the timing works out so that each thread grabs its first lock before either grabs its second, both threads block forever.
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785408559204-367470827.png
blocks.alt: A Simple Concrete Example: Two Threads, Two Locks

blocks.title: The classic textbook case
blocks.content: This exact two thread, two lock pattern is the first deadlock most programmers ever meet, usually while writing multi threaded code that locks more than one resource.
3. Deadlock vs a Process That Is Merely Slow or Blocked
blocks.text: 3. Deadlock vs a Process That Is Merely Slow or Blocked

blocks.content: Being blocked is normal and temporary. A process waiting for disk input and output, a network reply, or a busy processor will eventually get what it needs and continue on its own. A deadlocked process is fundamentally different: it will never proceed by itself, no matter how long you wait, because the very thing it needs will never become free.
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785408559204-12816301.png
blocks.alt: Deadlock vs a Process That Is Merely Slow or Blocked

blocks.title: The key test
blocks.content: Ask whether the wait will end on its own given enough time. If yes, it is ordinary blocking. If no, without outside intervention such as killing a process, it is a deadlock.
4. A Real World Analogy: The Narrow Bridge
blocks.text: 4. A Real World Analogy: The Narrow Bridge

blocks.content: Picture a narrow bridge that fits only one car at a time, with a car entering from each end at once. Each driver waits politely for the other to reverse first, but neither one ever does. Both cars sit there indefinitely, each one blocking the only path the other could use to escape.
Two cars, one lane, and a silent standoff where reversing first feels like losing, so nobody moves at all.
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785408559204-673514121.png
blocks.alt: A Real World Analogy: The Narrow Bridge

blocks.content: 5. The Four Necessary Conditions

Researchers identified four conditions that must all hold at the same time for a deadlock to occur. Removing any single one of them makes deadlock impossible, which is exactly the idea behind prevention.

["Mutual exclusion: at least one resource must be held in a non shareable way, so only one process can use it at a time.","Hold and wait: a process is holding at least one resource while it waits to acquire another.","No preemption: a resource cannot be forcibly taken away from the process holding it, it must be released voluntarily.","Circular wait: a closed chain of processes exists, where each one is waiting for a resource held by the next process in the chain."]
items: Mutual exclusion: at least one resource must be held in a non shareable way, so only one process can use it at a time.
Hold and wait: a process is holding at least one resource while it waits to acquire another.
No preemption: a resource cannot be forcibly taken away from the process holding it, it must be released voluntarily.
Circular wait: a closed chain of processes exists, where each one is waiting for a resource held by the next process in the chain.

blocks.title: Just a preview
blocks.content: This is only a short introduction to each condition. Full depth on all four, including proofs and worked examples, is covered in the dedicated Deadlocks module, in the Four Necessary Conditions topic.
6. How Deadlocks Are Handled, at a High Level
blocks.text: 6. How Deadlocks Are Handled, at a High Level

blocks.content: Operating systems and databases can deal with deadlocks in a few broad ways. They can prevent deadlocks by ruling out one of the four conditions, avoid them by carefully checking each resource request before granting it, or let them happen and then detect and recover from them afterward.

Many general purpose operating systems choose a fourth option: they simply ignore the problem, on the reasoning that deadlocks are rare enough and the cost of always preventing them is too high. This deliberate choice is nicknamed the ostrich algorithm.
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785408559205-987941992.png
blocks.alt: How Deadlocks Are Handled, at a High Level

blocks.title: Covered in depth elsewhere
blocks.content: Prevention, avoidance, the Bankers Algorithm, and detection and recovery each get a full topic of their own in the dedicated Deadlocks module.
7. Common Mistakes

["Confusing a deadlock with a process that is merely slow or running on a heavily loaded machine. A slow process is still making progress, a deadlocked one is not.","Assuming deadlocks are rare enough in practice to ignore entirely. They are a genuinely important concern in database systems and any concurrent program that uses more than one lock."]
items: Confusing a deadlock with a process that is merely slow or running on a heavily loaded machine. A slow process is still making progress, a deadlocked one is not.
Assuming deadlocks are rare enough in practice to ignore entirely. They are a genuinely important concern in database systems and any concurrent program that uses more than one lock.
